lesson.child_mission: A place can be described by its location (where it is), its features (what is there), how people use it and how it changes. Geographers describe what can be observed and measured before giving opinions.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same HSIE idea to a new place or source, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Describe your school ground using location, three features and two uses. Which sentence is an opinion instead of a feature?

FEEDBACK
For example: "The school ground is behind the main building" is location; "a basketball court" is a feature; "the best place" is an opinion.

WATCH FOR
Describing only what you like about a place gives opinions without the features other people could observe.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write a place profile of somewhere you know. Include its location with a nearby landmark and direction, six features, three uses and one change over time. Add a sketch or photo.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: Maple Creek Reserve is east of the town centre near Station Street. Features: a creek, bushland and picnic shelters. People use it for walking and bird watching. Opinion kept separate: "I find it peaceful".

TRY FIRST
Describe your school ground using location, three features and two uses. Which sentence is an opinion instead of a feature?

FEEDBACK
For example: "The school ground is behind the main building" is location; "a basketball court" is a feature; "the best place" is an opinion.
teach_steps.explain:
A place can be described by its location (where it is), its features (what is there), how people use it and how it changes. Geographers describe what can be observed and measured before giving opinions.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the sources, map features or community examples that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a detail is uncertain, identify what source you would need next. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
